questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine taxonomy using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher assigns a newly found fossil to a genus and species by comparing its anatomical traits with known specimens.

questions.stem: Which statement about taxonomy is best supported by the account?

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine species concepts using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: Two fossils look similar in tooth shape but differ in body size and limb proportions, prompting debate over whether they are one species or two.

questions.stem: The evidence most strongly supports which claim about species concepts?

options.text: Species are always defined by the ability to interbreed, even for extinct fossils where this cannot be tested.
options.misconception: The disagreement shows that species decisions depend on which criteria and evidence are emphasized.

options.text: Species boundaries in fossils are always obvious and never debated.
options.misconception: It imposes an arbitrary rule that would split every variable population.

questions.explanation: It denies the well-known debates that characterize fossil taxonomy.
questions.hint: Paleontologists often use morphological species concepts and explicitly discuss uncertainty.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine radiometric dating using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher assigns a newly found fossil to a genus and species by comparing its anatomical traits with known specimens.

questions.stem: How should taxonomy be understood in this context?

options.text: Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing, and classifying organisms based on their characteristics and relationships.
Taxonomy is the dating of fossils using radioactive decay measurements.
options.misconception: The researcher is classifying the fossil by comparing its anatomy with established groups.

options.text: Taxonomy is the reconstruction of the ancient environment from pollen grains.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to dating, which answers a different question.

options.text: Taxonomy is the excavation technique used to remove a fossil from rock.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to palynology, the study of pollen.

questions.explanation: It assigns the work to excavation, which is field technique rather than classification.
questions.hint: Classification is a first step that allows researchers to compare finds and discuss relationships.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine species concepts using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: Two fossils look similar in tooth shape but differ in body size and limb proportions, prompting debate over whether they are one species or two.

questions.stem: What is the best reading of species concepts here?

options.text: Species are always defined by the ability to interbreed, even for extinct fossils where this cannot be tested.
options.misconception: The disagreement shows that species decisions depend on which criteria and evidence are emphasized.

options.text: Species concepts provide criteria for deciding whether fossil forms belong to one species or separate species, and different concepts can yield different groupings.
Any two fossils that differ in any measurement must belong to different species.
options.misconception: It applies the biological species concept to fossils where interbreeding cannot be observed.

options.text: Species boundaries in fossils are always obvious and never debated.
options.misconception: It imposes an arbitrary rule that would split every variable population.

questions.explanation: It denies the well-known debates that characterize fossil taxonomy.
questions.hint: Paleontologists often use morphological species concepts and explicitly discuss uncertainty.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine cladistics using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher builds a branching diagram in which shared derived traits define nested groups, and chooses the tree requiring the fewest changes.

questions.stem: Which account of cladistics is most consistent with the facts?

options.text: Cladistics groups organisms by overall similarity regardless of evolutionary history.
options.misconception: The branching diagram uses shared derived traits to infer relationships and prefers the simplest tree.

options.text: Cladistics is a method for dating fossils by measuring radioactive isotopes.
options.misconception: It confuses cladistics with phenetics, which groups by overall similarity.

options.text: Cladistics classifies organisms by shared derived characteristics and seeks the simplest evolutionary tree consistent with the evidence.
Cladistics arranges species in a single linear sequence from primitive to advanced.
options.misconception: It assigns the method to dating, a different analytical task.

questions.explanation: It describes a ladder-like progression, whereas cladistics produces branching trees.
questions.hint: Parsimony favors the tree requiring the fewest independent changes, a standard cladistic criterion.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine hominin phylogeny using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A diagram shows several hominin branches, with some lineages ending without descendants and one leading to modern humans.

questions.stem: Which statement about hominin phylogeny is best supported by the account?

options.text: A hominin phylogeny is a straight line of progress from ape to human with no side branches.
options.misconception: The diagram presents branching relationships, including extinct side branches and one line to us.

options.text: A hominin phylogeny is a chart of the geographic locations where fossils were found.
options.misconception: It describes an outdated ladder model, not a branching tree.

options.text: A hominin phylogeny is a list of fossils sorted by their numerical age alone.
options.misconception: It confuses relationships with a simple distribution map.

options.text: A hominin phylogeny is a branching hypothesis about the evolutionary relationships among human-lineage species.

questions.explanation: It reduces phylogeny to age ordering, ignoring inferred ancestry.
questions.hint: Evolution produces trees with many branches, most of which end in extinction.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine stratigraphy using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: An excavation records the order and composition of sediment layers, noting that deeper layers were deposited earlier under undisturbed conditions.

questions.stem: Which choice correctly identifies stratigraphy in this case?

options.misconception: The recorded layer order lets the team establish which finds are earlier and which are later.

options.text: Stratigraphy is the study of layered deposits to establish the relative order of events and finds.

options.misconception: It assigns the work to chemical analysis of bone, a different technique.

options.text: Stratigraphy is the reconstruction of an animal's diet from its tooth shape.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to bathymetry, the measurement of water depth.

questions.explanation: It assigns the work to dietary reconstruction, which uses different evidence.
questions.hint: The law of superposition allows deeper undisturbed layers to be read as earlier.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine radiometric dating using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A volcanic ash layer above a fossil is analyzed for the decay of an isotope with a known half-life, yielding a numerical age for the layer.

questions.stem: What does radiometric dating most directly reveal about the community?

options.text: Radiometric dating establishes only which layer is older than another without numerical ages.
options.misconception: The decay measurement yields a numerical age for the volcanic layer and brackets the fossil.

options.text: Radiometric dating can be applied only to organic materials such as wood or bone.
options.misconception: It describes relative dating, which gives order rather than numerical age.

options.text: Radiometric dating estimates numerical ages by measuring the decay of radioactive isotopes at known rates.
Radiometric dating gives an age by comparing the fossil to similar fossils elsewhere.
options.misconception: It restricts the method to organic material, whereas many methods date minerals.

questions.explanation: It confuses dating with typological comparison, a different approach.
questions.hint: A known half-life converts the parent-to-daughter ratio into an estimate in years.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine morphology using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher measures the shape of a fossil's jaw and the wear on its teeth to infer how it processed food.

questions.stem: Which inference about morphology is warranted here?

options.text: Morphology is the study of the chemical elements present in a fossil after burial.
options.misconception: The researcher uses jaw shape and tooth wear to draw inferences about diet and adaptation.

options.text: Morphology is the reconstruction of the climate of a region from tree rings.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to geochemistry, a different kind of analysis.

options.text: Morphology is the dating of a fossil using the decay of radioactive isotopes.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to dendroclimatology, the study of tree rings.

options.text: Morphology is the study of the form and structure of organisms, used with fossils to infer function and relationship.

questions.explanation: It assigns the work to dating, which answers a different question.
questions.hint: Form often reflects function, which is why morphology is informative about behavior.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine hominin diversity using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: Fossils from a single region and time span show several distinct hominin forms with different diets and body sizes living near one another.

questions.stem: The account above best illustrates which point about hominin diversity?

options.text: Several hominin species or distinct populations can coexist, so the human lineage was once more diverse than it is today.
Only one hominin species has ever existed at any given time in any region.
options.misconception: The finds show multiple forms with different adaptations living in the same area and period.

options.text: All fossil differences within a region are just variation within a single modern human population.
options.misconception: It denies the documented overlap of multiple hominin forms, contradicted by the finds.

options.text: Hominin diversity ended only with the invention of agriculture.
options.misconception: It collapses genuine distinct forms into a single living species without evidence.

questions.explanation: It proposes an unsupported and much later endpoint for a much earlier pattern.
questions.hint: A branching lineage means that multiple forms can coexist and compete.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine ancient DNA using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A geneticist extracts and sequences degraded DNA from an old bone, then compares it with genomes of living and archaic humans.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of ancient DNA fits the evidence?

options.text: Ancient DNA is a method for dating a fossil by the amount of DNA it contains.
options.misconception: The sequences allow direct comparison of archaic and modern genomes and tests of interbreeding.

options.text: Ancient DNA analysis can recover genetic material from old remains to test relationships and admixture directly.
Ancient DNA can only be recovered from fossils that are younger than a century.
options.misconception: It confuses DNA analysis with dating, which uses isotope decay.

options.text: Ancient DNA studies have shown that archaic humans made no genetic contribution to living people.
options.misconception: It imposes an arbitrary time limit that the field has surpassed.

questions.explanation: It denies documented archaic contribution to living human genomes.
questions.hint: Genetic evidence has revealed interbreeding that morphology alone could not detect.
